title: Where do we stop when we write equivalent fractions?
description: Three fourths and seven tenths are compared by writing both with the same fractional unit. The bottom numbers are multiplied to get a number both can reach, and then the top numbers are compared. Keeko doubts the answer by choosing the fraction with the bigger numbers.
teaching_notes: One idea: multiply the two bottom numbers to get a bottom number that both fractions can reach, then compare the top numbers. Watch for students who pick the fraction with the bigger numbers in it.

source: Compare 3/4 and 7/10 by finding equivalent fractions with th
video_script.why: A learner knows where to stop when writing equivalent fractions: at the number made by multiplying the two bottom numbers.
video_script.substitution: the book's own pair three fourths and seven tenths, with the book's two friends
video_script.anchor: the pair three fourths and seven tenths from the sugarcane juice groups
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says seven tenths is bigger because seven and ten are bigger numbers than three and four, and does not make the units the same.
video_script.payoff_line: three fourths is greater than seven tenths

final_answer.spoken: three fourths is thirty fortieths and seven tenths is twenty-eight fortieths, and thirty fortieths is more, so three fourths is greater than seven tenths

video_script.fraction_reading: three fourths, seven tenths, thirty fortieths, twenty-eight fortieths, fifteen twentieths, fourteen twentieths

names.{{NAME_3}}: the child who suggests going on till forty
names.{{NAME_4}}: the child who writes the equivalent fractions

never_show: a tick on 7/10 before the working
maths_rules: multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number gives an equivalent fraction
4 x 10 = 40, and 40 is a multiple of 4 and of 10
slip: Keeko says 7/10 is bigger because 7 and 10 are bigger numbers than 3 and 4; but 7/10 = 28/40 < 30/40
video_script.design: The pair stays on the board. The two bottom numbers are multiplied to find where both fractions meet, at forty. Then the top numbers thirty and twenty-eight are compared.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; 3/4 = 6/8 = 9/12 = 12/16 = 15/20 ... written one after another and 7/10 = 14/20 = 21/30 ... beside it; the words when do we stop? appear

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is from your book, where two friends compare three fourths and seven tenths.
<bookmark mark='list'/>{{NAME_4}} writes equivalent fractions of three fourths, one after another.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>When do we stop making equivalent fractions?

beats.on_screen: the list holds still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: 3/4 = (3 x 10)/(4 x 10) with the multiplier 10 circled; a note says same amount, new fractional unit; 3/4 and 7/10 sit side by side with different bottom numbers

marks.rule: 3/4 changes to (3 x 10)/(4 x 10) with the multiplier circled and the note same amount, new fractional unit
marks.need: 3/4 and 7/10 sit side by side with the bottom numbers circled in different colours

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number gives an equivalent fraction. The amount stays the same, but the fractional unit changes.
<bookmark mark='need'/>Three fourths and seven tenths have different bottom numbers. We stop when the two bottom numbers match.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the two fractions are three fourths and seven tenths.

beats.on_screen: To find: which is greater, using equivalent fractions with the same fractional unit
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find which is greater, using equivalent fractions with the same fractional unit.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: 4 x 10 = 40; 40 is a multiple of 4 and of 10, so both fractions can reach the bottom number 40

marks.stop: 4 x 10 = 40 is written and 40 is circled
marks.both: the words 40 is a multiple of 4 and of 10 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='stop'/>Step one, {{NAME_3}} suggests we go on till four times ten. That is forty.
<bookmark mark='both'/>Forty is a multiple of both four and ten, so both fractions can reach it.

marks.mul: the top and the bottom of 3/4 are multiplied by 10

narration: <bookmark mark='mul'/>Step two, multiply the top and the bottom of three fourths by ten.
<bookmark mark='res'/>Three times ten over four times ten is thirty fortieths.

marks.mul: the top and the bottom of 7/10 are multiplied by 4

narration: <bookmark mark='mul'/>Step three, multiply the top and the bottom of seven tenths by four.
<bookmark mark='res'/>Seven times four over ten times four is twenty-eight fortieths.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: both in fortieths; compare the numbers of fortieths: 30 and 28

marks.cmp: 30 fortieth pieces and 28 fortieth pieces are lined up one above the other

narration: <bookmark mark='cmp'/>Step four, both fractions are counted in fortieths, so we compare the number of fortieths. One has thirty, and the other has twenty-eight.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>Thirty fortieths is more than twenty-eight fortieths, so three fourths is greater than seven tenths.
<bookmark mark='twenty'/>Twenty works too, since fifteen twentieths is more than fourteen twentieths.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside 3/4 and 7/10
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: a bubble says 7/10 is bigger because 7 and 10 are bigger numbers than 3 and 4; 28/40 and 30/40 are shown and 28/40 is shorter; the bubble is struck out

marks.doubt: the bubble with the wrong idea appears
marks.look: the bubble shakes while the big numbers 7 and 10 are circled
marks.fix: 28/40 and 30/40 appear as two bars and the shorter bar is 28/40; the bubble is struck out

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks seven tenths is bigger, because seven and ten are bigger numbers than three and four.
<bookmark mark='look'/>Big numbers on the top and the bottom do not tell us the size of a fraction.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Seven tenths is only twenty-eight fortieths, which is less than thirty fortieths.
